cells.tense: You are holding what people handed you and you have set down the pieces that went stale.
cells.ask: Name one shared thing you still keep — a tradition, a story, a way of doing it — and say out loud why it's worth keeping.
cells.core:
You still hold what was handed to you. The ways, the stories, the way things get done. Some of it doesn't serve the people you're with anymore, and you sort that out without flinching. You've put down what needed putting down. What's left, you hold on purpose. That kind of bearing does work you don't announce. People lean on it without knowing they're leaning. When you move from one group toward another, you shape what goes with you and what stays behind. You don't grip what's finished and you don't rush the leaving. Things pass hand to hand, and you're one of the hands.

What keeps you steady here isn't luck. When you're at your center, hard things get held without a crack in you. The invitation this balance offers is yours to take or not — feed the quiet more, or spend it where it lands. Either way, standing there keeps working.
cells.sheetLine: You choose what goes with you and what stays behind.
cells.place: where you stand and hold what's handed to you

cells.tense: You are bracing for a separation that has not happened yet and may not be yours to bear.
cells.ask: Count what is actually yours to hold. Name one thing you're carrying for someone else, and give that one back this week.
cells.core:
You're already packing. Something still in front of you, a goodbye maybe, or a group you haven't left, and you're standing there loaded like it already went wrong. You keep hauling the old ways past where they still serve anyone, holding the shape of something that moved on already. Enduring ahead of the moment is a job you gave yourself. Nobody asked. The bearing is real. It's just being spent on what hasn't arrived. Building the bridge before you reach the bank is its own weight. There's a scene where people hear you, where the group shifts easily, and you're already rehearsing the worst turn. All that hauling keeps you from the crossing. That's the cost. Pushing toward a fixed ending is eating the actual going.

The person you're carrying for can hold something too. Hand one load back this week and find out.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing for a goodbye that hasn't happened.
cells.place: where you stand and hold what's handed to you

cells.tense: You stopped at a doorway that is already behind you and you are still standing there.
cells.ask: Ask one honest question about how another person sees the shared thing — and let their answer sit without defending or agreeing.
cells.core: The group moved on, or the belief did, and you stayed at the frame. Someone is still living by what you stopped passing down, or a way of doing things continues in your name and you've stepped out of it. Either way, you went quiet. Being the one who holds what a group shares is not a job you can go numb through. The pattern is what's missing. When you look at how people stuck together and how they broke, what made one group hold and another scatter, the answer isn't in your body. It's in how you read the thing. Start there. Notice what actually makes a group stay together, and say it plainly to someone. Naming the shape of it can put your hands back on the load.
cells.sheetLine: Plenty of weight to hold, none of it in your hands.
cells.place: where you stand and hold what's handed to you

cells.tense: You are already moving people through one shared thing to the next and calling it nothing.
cells.ask: Say out loud that one thing you do to keep people connected is yours, and not just how things are done.
cells.core: You're the one holding the group's continuity, the one who remembers what matters and passes it along, but you'd say you're just being normal. Somebody has to keep the thread. You do it. That's not a small job, and you do it under a shrug. The quiet goes unrecognized because you're the one calling it quiet. People feel steadied around you. You built that. When you're at center, the bearing gets easier, but nobody gets there on a shrug. Stop treating your own contribution like the background. The work doesn't need a shrine — just an owner who says, yes, that's mine. Once you claim it, standing there gets lighter because it stops being invisible.
cells.sheetLine: It's already yours. Nobody said so — including you.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is at a threshold of belonging right now — the record can only say the capacity for endurance is at a particular level, not what it has carried or is about to leave. The reader could reasonably say 'I'm not on the verge of anything, I'm just tired and holding too much.' If my read is wrong, the asks still stand: naming one shared thing you're keeping, counting what's actually yours to hold, asking a question instead of repeating, and putting down one communal burden all work regardless. The sentence that serves me more than the person is 'you're already on the bridge' — nobody can prove that from outside, so I've dropped it and let the mechanism carry the weight instead.
